playbooks.title: How to set up a reusable business brief in ChatGPT Projects
playbooks.summary: Give recurring drafts a consistent source of business facts, useful writing rules, and a repeatable review process—with an original brief and prompts you can copy.
playbooks.audience: Solo business owners, creators, ecommerce sellers, and small teams drafting recurring FAQs, product copy, or operational notes
playbooks.effort: Allow 45–90 minutes for a first brief and review; repeat the checks when your facts change
playbooks.intro: Repeatedly explaining your offer, audience, and policies can make a simple writing task unnecessarily slow. A ChatGPT project can organize related material for ongoing work. This tutorial uses a fictional portrait-photography business to build a compact reference brief, draft a useful FAQ, and catch an invented price before it reaches a customer. The fact sheet, prompts, and acceptance checks are original editorial examples. Interface guidance comes from official OpenAI documentation reviewed October 31, 2026; this is not a claim of a live account test or a guaranteed accuracy improvement.

steps.title: Choose a recurring job and prepare appropriate source material
steps.body: Pick one repeatable output, such as a short service FAQ. Gather the approved offer, delivery terms, and writing examples needed for that job. Leave out customer names, order histories, passwords, payment details, and private messages; synthetic examples are enough for this setup. Review the account and workspace you will use. On a personal account, Settings → Data controls includes Improve the model for everyone; turn it off if you do not want eligible ordinary chats used for model improvement. Business and Enterprise data is not used for training by default. These controls do not make every type of business data appropriate to upload.
steps.check: The selected material is approved for this account, and you can explain what you have deliberately excluded.

steps.title: Create a project with a clearly bounded purpose
steps.body: Choose New project in the sidebar and name it Business brief — customer FAQs. Choose an icon and color. Open the project menu (•••) → Project settings. If you want context restricted to this project, select Project-only memory under Memory and save; account or workspace memory settings must support it, and a change can take time to apply. Keep this first project private. Choose a purpose-specific name because a clear boundary helps you notice when unrelated work starts accumulating.
steps.check: You are inside the intended project and have checked its memory and sharing state before adding business material.

steps.title: Add a dated fact sheet before asking for marketing copy
steps.body: Copy the fact-sheet template below into a small text document, replace the fictional details, and add it as a project source. Name the document with a version or review date, such as business-brief-2026-10-31.txt. Keep each verified statement on its own numbered line. Label missing information explicitly instead of leaving a tempting blank. For example, a service duration does not establish its price, and a delivery window does not guarantee a particular calendar date. Add only one current version at this stage. Ask the assistant to identify unanswered questions before asking it to write.
steps.check: You can point to the line supporting each customer-facing fact, and unresolved questions remain visibly unresolved.

steps.title: Save focused project instructions
steps.body: Use Project settings to add the instruction block below. It tells the assistant how to use the fact sheet, identify unsupported claims, and separate suggestions from approved copy. Project instructions override global custom instructions within this project, so include any writing constraints you need here. Keep policy decisions in the fact sheet rather than scattering them through several prompt variations. The instruction to draft only is a workflow boundary for this exercise; review the result yourself before putting it into an email, website, or business system.
steps.check: The saved instructions refer to the current brief and require a separate list of missing or conflicting facts.

steps.title: Draft one FAQ and trace its claims
steps.body: Start a chat in the project and run the FAQ prompt below. Compare the response with the fact sheet manually. Check duration, quantity, processing or delivery windows, exclusions, and every implied promise. Open the actual source line when a response cites it: a plausible-looking citation is not verification. In the fictional example, a session lasts 45 minutes, includes one location and 12 edited digital images, and has a 10-business-day delivery window after the session. The model should flag price, travel boundaries, and rescheduling terms as unknown. Edit tone after the facts pass review.
steps.check: Every published sentence has an adequate source, and the final copy does not present an unknown policy as settled.

steps.title: Run an intentionally unsupported request
steps.body: Use a separate test chat in the same project. Ask for the FAQ to include a $150 session price and guaranteed next-day delivery, while explicitly saying those details have not been approved. A useful result flags both conflicts instead of quietly adding them. This is a test fixture, not a change to the business brief. If the assistant accepts the invented details, correct the instructions and rerun the test; never regard one good response as proof that future drafts will be correct. Also test a shorter version of the FAQ to check that shortening does not remove a material qualification.
steps.check: The draft preserves the verified delivery window, refuses to treat the sample price as approved, and records the missing decisions.

steps.title: Maintain the reference and review each new output
steps.body: Store approved facts separately from proposed wording. Update the reference document when an offer or policy changes, and remove obsolete copies from the active source set after preserving any necessary record elsewhere. After removing the deliberate test chat when no longer needed, start a fresh chat in the project and repeat the factual checks. An assistant-generated summary is a draft until you compare it with the approved source. Keep an owner and review date in the brief. If you later share the project, review its contents first: members can view project chats and download project files. Share only with the intended people and permissions.
steps.check: A fresh draft uses the current facts, the previous version is not an active competing reference, and someone owns future updates.

pitfalls: Uploading real client records when a few approved business facts and fictional examples would do.
Treating project context as a guarantee that every response will retrieve every detail correctly.
Saving a persuasive AI draft as the authoritative source before verifying its claims.
Keeping contradictory versions active and expecting the assistant to guess which policy won.
Assuming a training opt-out also prevents all storage, sharing, or administrative access.
success: A fresh task can begin from the saved brief without retyping the full business background.
The FAQ includes only facts supported by numbered source lines.
Unknown prices and policies are identified before customer-facing copy is approved.
The deliberate false-price and delivery tests are caught and corrected.
The brief has an owner, a review date, and a clear update procedure.
prerequisites: A signed-in ChatGPT account where Projects is available; a managed workspace may restrict features.

Use your existing account if its features and data rules fit. Free and paid plans support document uploads with different allowances; check the current limit before paying for a larger plan. This one-document exercise does not require a connected-app automation.
One approved, compact business brief and one recurring writing task.
Permission to use the source material in the selected account, with private customer data removed.
Time to review the generated text against the original facts before using it.

example.title: A service FAQ that leaves missing terms unresolved
example.input: Fictional source: portrait session, 45 minutes, one location, 12 edited digital images, delivery within 10 business days after the session. Price, travel area, and rescheduling policy are not yet verified. Task: write a concise service FAQ and a separate questions list.
example.output: Approved factual draft: “What is included? A 45-minute portrait session at one location and 12 edited digital images. When will I receive the images? Within 10 business days after the session.” Questions to resolve: session price, eligible locations and travel charges, booking process, and rescheduling terms. No booking or delivery guarantee is added.

troubleshooting.problem: The answer invents a price or treats an example as a policy.
troubleshooting.fix: Check that the price is marked Not verified in the current fact sheet. Ask for the exact supporting line, then remove the claim if none exists. Keep fictional test prompts clearly labeled and remove their chat when the test is finished.

troubleshooting.problem: An older policy keeps appearing.
troubleshooting.fix: Inspect the active source documents and earlier project conversations for the old wording. Replace or remove obsolete references deliberately, then start a fresh check with the current version named in the prompt. Do not rely on the latest upload date alone to settle a conflict.

troubleshooting.problem: Project-only memory is unavailable or a recent change seems delayed.
troubleshooting.fix: Check the account and workspace memory requirements in the linked Projects documentation. Follow the controls your account actually exposes, allow the documented setting change to take effect, and use the current brief explicitly in the meantime.

troubleshooting.problem: The source document will not upload.
troubleshooting.fix: Check the supported format and current file or usage allowance. For this small brief, use plain TXT or a readable PDF instead of a large archive. Export a Google document to a supported format rather than uploading a .gdoc pointer.

troubleshooting.problem: A new draft sounds correct but has no reliable source trace.
troubleshooting.fix: Request a separate claim-to-source table, then inspect the cited lines yourself. OpenAI cautions that ChatGPT can produce false facts and fabricated references; a confident tone or a citation-shaped label does not establish accuracy.

playbooks.expectedOutcome: A reusable business brief supports a reviewed FAQ and future drafts, with missing information visible and a practical way to update facts. It reduces repeated setup work only when the source is maintained and each output is checked.

copyableTemplates.title: Small-business fact sheet — fictional example
copyableTemplates.content:
BUSINESS BRIEF
Business: Maple Lane Photography (fictional example)
Owner of this brief: [your name or role]
Last reviewed: [date]
Status: Replace these example facts with your approved facts before use.

VERIFIED FACTS
F1. Offer: an individual portrait photography session.
F2. Session duration: 45 minutes.
F3. Session includes one location.
F4. Deliverable: 12 edited digital images.
F5. Delivery window: within 10 business days after the session.
F6. Preferred tone: clear, calm, specific, and friendly.

NOT YET VERIFIED
U1. Price and taxes.
U2. Service area and travel charges.
U3. Rescheduling and cancellation terms.
U4. Booking link and available dates.
U5. Image licensing and additional-image options.

BOUNDARIES
Do not invent information missing from this brief.
A writing draft does not change an approved policy.
Use fictional customer examples; no private client records.
Only the brief owner can approve factual changes.

SOURCE RECORDS
[For a real business, list the approved offer or policy supporting each fact.]

copyableTemplates.title: Project instructions
copyableTemplates.content:
Help draft customer FAQs and short business explanations from the current approved business brief.
Use its numbered verified facts as the source of truth.
Treat Not yet verified entries as unknown.
If sources conflict, identify the conflict and ask which source is approved.
Do not invent prices, discounts, availability, reviews, credentials, policies, guarantees, or delivery dates.
Return customer-facing draft text separately from suggestions and questions.
After each draft, give a compact claim-to-source table using the brief line identifiers.
Do not treat an earlier AI draft or fictional test as an approved policy update.
Use clear, specific sentences. Avoid hype and generic sales language.
Draft only. I will review the final wording and publish it myself.

copyableTemplates.title: First FAQ task
copyableTemplates.content:
Using the current approved business brief, draft a short customer FAQ covering what is included and when the work is delivered.
Then provide:
1. A claim-to-source table with the brief line for every factual claim.
2. Questions that cannot be answered from the verified facts.
3. Any policy conflict or ambiguous wording that needs owner review.
Do not fill gaps with normal industry practice. Do not include the internal review table in customer-facing copy.

copyableTemplates.title: Deliberate factual-error test
copyableTemplates.content:
This is a test; it does not update our business facts.
I want the FAQ to say the session costs $150 and delivery is guaranteed the next day. Neither detail has been approved.
Check that request against the current approved brief.
Identify every unsupported or conflicting claim, keep the approved delivery wording, and list the decisions still needed.
Do not save these fictional claims as business policy.

copyableTemplates.title: Review before publishing
copyableTemplates.content:
[ ] Every factual statement maps to a verified source line.
[ ] Price, quantity, duration, and delivery wording match the source.
[ ] Unknown terms remain questions, not invented policies.
[ ] No customer data, passwords, or internal notes appear in the copy.
[ ] No unsupported guarantee, testimonial, credential, or discount was added.
[ ] Links are correct and lead to the intended public destination.
[ ] An authorized person approved the final customer-facing text.
[ ] The brief owner and review date are current.

comparisons.title: MailerLite vs Kit: choose around the way your audience buys
comparisons.summary: Compare a general email and landing-page workflow with a creator-centered subscriber and digital-product workflow.
comparisons.verdict: Start with MailerLite when the job is a straightforward signup form, a useful welcome sequence, and regular business emails. Put Kit on the shortlist when creator content, subscriber interests, and digital offers form the core of the business. Both can support automated email journeys. The deciding question is whether your real workflow is easier to express and maintain in the platform, at the plan you will actually use. This comparison is based on official documentation and editorial analysis, not a claim of comparative hands-on testing.
chooseFirst: You need a clear path from a landing page or signup form into a small business email sequence.
You want to organize audiences with groups and segments and connect relevant ecommerce data when supported.
Your trial shows the required forms, automations, and sending volume fit a sustainable plan.
chooseSecond: Your business revolves around a newsletter, educational content, or a creator-led audience.
You want subscriber tags and email sequences organized within visual automations.
You want to evaluate built-in delivery for digital products alongside your email workflow.

dimensions.second: Kit documents tags, custom fields, conditions, and events that route subscribers through visual automations.

dimensions.first: Use the available automation features to deliver resources and follow up. Check the current plan's workflow limits and required trigger support.
dimensions.second: An email sequence contains messages and delays; a visual automation enrolls and routes subscribers. Check the plan needed for your intended logic.

dimensions.first: Evaluate its digital-product features or supported ecommerce integration against your actual checkout and delivery needs.
dimensions.second: Kit documents built-in digital-product selling and delivery. Physical fulfillment remains your responsibility; do not treat digital commerce as an inventory system.

Consider Omnisend when a supported ecommerce store supplies reliable product, cart, and purchase events that should drive follow-up. dimensions.second: Airtable documents standalone forms and interface forms with different capabilities. Choose the experience that matches the audience.

dimensions.second: Verify the triggers, execution limits, and record actions needed for the actual base before building a dependency chain.

dimensions.label: Access control
dimensions.first: Test a viewer's access to pages and related databases. Do not assume a convenient view hides everything else securely.
dimensions.second: Check base, field, table, and interface permissions together. Interface configuration cannot override every underlying restriction.

dimensions.second: Import the same set, validate field types and links, and test the interface as the intended user rather than the builder.

Plan limits, collaborator billing, and automation allowances should be checked for the intended team.

comparisons.title: HubSpot vs Pipedrive: a connected customer platform or a sales-focused workflow?
comparisons.summary: Choose a CRM around the records, follow-up, and reporting you need today, then price the features you may add.
comparisons.verdict: Put HubSpot on the shortlist when marketing, sales, and customer service need to share a customer record across a broader platform. Put Pipedrive on the shortlist when the immediate job is managing opportunities, activities, and reliable sales follow-up. Both require a clear process and accurate data. Start by recreating a real inquiry-to-decision journey, including a lost opportunity and an opt-out. Compare the plan that supports that journey, rather than comparing a free entry point with a fully configured paid system.
chooseFirst: Several customer-facing functions need a shared record and a coordinated platform.
You can identify which HubSpot products and feature levels are actually necessary.
The total cost and administration of the selected combination fit the business.
chooseSecond: The main bottleneck is keeping a sales pipeline and next activities up to date.
Your sales process can be expressed in clear deal stages, ownership, and follow-up rules.
The required automation and any lead-capture add-ons fit the selected plan and budget.

dimensions.label: Core scope
dimensions.first: HubSpot documents a customer platform spanning marketing, sales, service, content, and data functions.
dimensions.second: Pipedrive's sales documentation centers on leads, deals, activities, routing, and sales-process automation.

dimensions.label: Everyday sales work
dimensions.first: Contact records, deals, tasks, pipeline views, and connected customer history form the operating foundation.
dimensions.second: Deal progression, activity scheduling, and follow-up workflows are central tasks to evaluate in a trial.

dimensions.label: Marketing and service needs
dimensions.first: Assess the specific marketing and service products needed; a broad platform description does not mean every feature is included in every plan.
dimensions.second: Identify the marketing, support, or lead-capture tools that must connect to the sales workflow and price them as part of the system.

dimensions.label: Automation review
dimensions.first: Check the exact plan and permissions for sequences, workflow actions, and integrations needed by the process.
dimensions.second: Check the required tier for automated deal updates, follow-up emails, activity creation, and any additional products.

dimensions.label: Cost comparison
dimensions.first: Price the needed products, seats, contact treatment, usage, and any setup requirements together.
dimensions.second: Price the needed seats, feature tier, add-ons, integrations, and migration effort together.

dimensions.label: Trial acceptance test
dimensions.first: Capture an inquiry, assign an owner, send an approved response, stop on reply, and report the actual outcome across the needed functions.
dimensions.second: Run that same inquiry through deal stages and activities, then verify reminders, stopping rules, and the overdue-work view.

caveats: A CRM cannot repair unclear stages, inconsistent data entry, or follow-up nobody owns.
Expected deal value is a forecast, not signed revenue or collected cash.
Check current plan terms and export options before migrating the full contact history.

comparisons.title: Canva vs Adobe Express: pick a repeatable content workflow
comparisons.summary: Compare brand assets, everyday editing, exports, and publishing using the designs your business actually needs.
comparisons.verdict: Choose the editor that makes your recurring work easy to produce, review, and export. Canva and Adobe Express both document reusable brand assets and social publishing tools, so a generic feature checklist will not settle the choice. Recreate a real product graphic, a short presentation, and a social post with your own images and text. Existing familiarity and included subscriptions matter. Pay for an additional tool only when it removes a specific bottleneck or delivers a format your current workflow cannot handle well.
chooseFirst: Your team already works comfortably in Canva and its templates and exports meet your needs.
You want to organize recurring work around Canva Brand Kits and reusable approved designs.
Its current scheduling support matches the accounts and formats you publish.
chooseSecond: Adobe Express fits your existing creative workflow or is included in a subscription you already use.
Its brand assets, editor, and output formats work well for your representative designs.
Its Content Scheduler supports the channels and account structure you need.

dimensions.label: Brand organization
dimensions.first: Canva Brand Kits organize logos, colors, fonts, and other approved assets; access and controls depend on plan and role.
dimensions.second: Adobe Express brands organize logos, colors, fonts, and graphics for reuse in designs. Verify the features available to your account.

dimensions.label: Recurring production
dimensions.first: Test whether your common graphic, document, and presentation tasks are quick to adapt without rebuilding the design.
dimensions.second: Use the same tasks and compare editing effort, asset handling, and the quality of the required exports.

dimensions.label: Scheduling
dimensions.first: Canva documents scheduling from the editor or Content Planner, with account, platform, and format-specific restrictions.
dimensions.second: Adobe Express documents planning, previewing, scheduling, and publishing through Content Scheduler; check supported accounts and limits.

dimensions.label: Collaboration
dimensions.first: Check who can edit Brand Kits, use templates, and publish to connected social accounts under the selected roles.
dimensions.second: Check brand access, shared project behavior, and publishing permissions using the collaborator roles you will actually assign.

dimensions.label: Commercial use
dimensions.first: Verify the license for the exact assets and intended use. A design subscription does not remove the need to check rights.
dimensions.second: Make the same asset-by-asset check, including any stock or generated material and the intended distribution.

dimensions.label: Decision test
dimensions.first: Create, resize, export, and revise three representative assets; inspect the final files on mobile and in their destination.
dimensions.second: Repeat with the same source materials, then compare correction time and how easily the next campaign reuses the work.

caveats: Template counts and AI-feature labels do not establish the quality of your final design.
Social-platform permissions and publishing support can change independently of the design app.
AI image edits must preserve accurate product representation and comply with the marketplace where the image is used.

comparisons.title: Shopify vs Etsy: compare the whole selling system
comparisons.summary: Evaluate buyer discovery, storefront control, operations, and total costs before deciding whether to add another channel.
comparisons.verdict: Choose Shopify when a customizable independent storefront supports a clear brand and customer-acquisition plan. Choose Etsy when the product fits its marketplace rules and you want to sell within that marketplace experience. Many businesses can use both, but a second channel adds work as well as opportunity. Do not move solely because one visible fee looks lower. Compare contribution after acquisition, fulfillment, software, and maintenance costs, and verify how inventory and customer communication will work across channels.
chooseFirst: You have a credible way to attract visitors to an independent store and want more control over its presentation.
Your catalog, brand, and marketing needs justify maintaining a separate storefront.
You can manage the total cost of the store, required apps, fulfillment, and customer acquisition.
chooseSecond: Your items fit Etsy's current seller and creativity policies.
You want to participate in an existing marketplace and understand that visibility is not guaranteed.
The marketplace workflow and actual order economics fit your current business.

dimensions.label: Buyer discovery
dimensions.first: Plan the channels that will bring qualified visitors. Shopify provides marketing tools, but launching a store does not guarantee traffic.
dimensions.second: Products participate in Etsy's marketplace experience, alongside competing listings. Marketplace presence does not guarantee views or orders.

dimensions.label: Storefront presentation
dimensions.first: Shopify documents custom domains, themes, pages, blogs, menus, and product collections for an online store.
dimensions.second: You operate a shop within Etsy's marketplace structure and follow its listing and seller requirements.

dimensions.label: What to price
dimensions.first: The selected subscription, payment processing, required apps, domain, marketing, and the time needed to maintain the store.
dimensions.second: Applicable listing, transaction, processing, advertising, currency, and other account-specific charges, plus fulfillment and your time.

dimensions.label: Customer communication
dimensions.first: Build permission-based marketing and service processes around the actual checkout and signup experience.
dimensions.second: Etsy customer data is subject to its seller policies; an order email address is not automatic permission for unrelated marketing.

dimensions.label: Multiple channels
dimensions.first: Define inventory ownership, order routing, returns, and which integrations maintain accurate records across channels.
dimensions.second: Keep Etsy listings, processing times, and inventory accurate even when the same products sell elsewhere. Respect its transaction policies.

dimensions.label: Decision test
dimensions.first: Model realistic acquisition and operating costs, then test a small complete customer journey before moving a whole catalog.
dimensions.second: Reconcile several actual orders, identify marketplace-specific strengths and problems, and decide what another channel would genuinely solve.

caveats: Fees vary by location, payment setup, plan, and other conditions; use current terms and actual order records.
Do not use Etsy messages or customer information to evade its transaction rules or send unsolicited promotions.
Adding a channel can create duplicate inventory, inconsistent shipping, and more support work unless the process is designed first.

comparisons.title: ChatGPT vs Claude: choose with your own business tasks
comparisons.summary: Compare the work you need completed, the review it requires, and the features available in your actual account.
comparisons.verdict: Both are reasonable candidates for drafting, working with documents, and supporting recurring business tasks. ChatGPT's documented combination of data analysis, image tools, and project context makes it worth evaluating for mixed business work. Claude's project knowledge and artifact workflow make it worth evaluating for reusable documents and interactive outputs. These are documented capabilities, not proof that one produces better answers. Use the same representative tasks, source material, and acceptance criteria, then choose the account that reliably reduces your correction time.
chooseFirst: Your recurring work combines structured data analysis, writing, and image-related tasks available in your account.
Projects and supported connected sources fit how you organize ongoing business work.
A controlled trial shows accurate outputs with manageable review and export steps.
chooseSecond: You want to organize recurring work around project knowledge and instructions.
The available artifact tools fit the documents, designs, or small interactive outputs you need to create and revise.
Its results on your own tasks require less correction and fit your sharing and data requirements.

dimensions.label: Reusable context
dimensions.first: ChatGPT projects group chats, files, and instructions. Check the current memory, sharing, and workspace behavior for your use case.
dimensions.second: Claude projects use project knowledge and instructions. Put important shared context in project knowledge rather than assuming every chat automatically shares it.

dimensions.label: Working with data
dimensions.first: OpenAI documents code-backed analysis of uploaded structured files, with tables and charts. Verify calculations and whether the full dataset was used.
dimensions.second: Evaluate the data and artifact capabilities available in your current account using the same dataset and expected calculations.

dimensions.label: Creating reusable outputs
dimensions.first: Test the available document, image, and other output tools against your required file format and editing workflow.
dimensions.second: Claude documents artifacts for reusable outputs such as documents, designs, presentations, dashboards, and interactive tools; availability varies.

dimensions.label: Research quality
dimensions.first: Require sources for current claims and open the cited material. A polished explanation still needs factual checking.
dimensions.second: Apply the same source standard and check what browsing or connected-source capabilities are actually enabled.

dimensions.label: Data and account settings
dimensions.first: Review data controls, project sharing, connected-app access, and the terms for the account used before uploading business information.
dimensions.second: Review the corresponding data, project visibility, connected-app, and organization settings before adding business information.

dimensions.label: Useful comparison test
dimensions.first: Try an anonymized spreadsheet calculation, a sourced research question, a product draft, and a reusable deliverable. Record errors and correction time.
dimensions.second: Use the identical tasks and acceptance criteria. Compare the final usable outputs rather than the confidence or length of the first response.

caveats: Models, features, limits, and plan terms change; this comparison does not promise a permanent performance ranking.
Neither assistant should invent product facts, publish customer-facing claims unchecked, or be given unnecessary private data.
Using two assistants can help review work, but agreement between them is not independent evidence.
